extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proofs, sequences/series, and basic set theory/cardinality
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter excerpt giving definitions, theorems, proofs, and exercises about convergence/divergence tests for infinite series and basic set cardinality (bijections, countable/uncountable sets, Cantor diagonalization, Cantor-Bernstein-Schroeder). Useful as a reference for proving or deciding convergence and comparing sizes of sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence test / term test for divergence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the series sum_{k=1}^∞ a_k converges, then the sequence a_k converges to 0. Contrapositive (corollary 13.1): If a_k does not converge to 0 (either diverges or converges to a non-zero number), then the series sum a_k diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This test only detects divergence: it shows some series diverge by checking their terms do not tend to 0, but it says nothing in general when a_k → 0 (series may or may not converge). Example: harmonic series diverges even though its terms go to 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric series convergence criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A geometric series has the form a + ar + ar^2 + ar^3 + ... with real a,r. If |r| < 1 then the geometric series converges (to a/(1-r)). If a ≠ 0 and |r| = 1 then the series diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise suggests using Example 13.10 as inspiration; the standard derivation uses partial sums s_n = a(1-r^{n})/(1-r) when r ≠ 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison test
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose {a_k} and {b_k} are series terms with 0 ≤ a_k ≤ b_k for each k. If sum b_k converges, then sum a_k converges. Also, if 0 ≤ b_k ≤ a_k for each k and sum b_k diverges, then sum a_k diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for comparing an unknown series to a known convergent/divergent benchmark. Requires nonnegativity of terms for the stated forms; proofs use monotonicity of partial sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit comparison test (special form presented)
rubrics_metrics.description: For series with positive terms a_k, b_k > 0, if lim_{k→∞} (a_k / b_k) = 0 and sum b_k converges, then sum a_k converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text suggests your proof may use previous exercises; note this is a special case of the usual limit-comparison test (if limit L with 0 < L < ∞ then convergence/divergence of one implies the other).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute convergence test
rubrics_metrics.description: If sum |a_k| converges (absolute convergence), then the series sum a_k converges (converges absolutely ⇒ converges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard proof uses Cauchy criterion or comparison of positive series; often used as an easy sufficient condition for convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratio test (for positive-term sequences as stated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a series sum a_k with each a_k positive, if lim_{k→∞} (a_{k+1}/a_k) = L < 1 then sum a_k converges. If L > 1 then sum a_k diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text allows using earlier exercises in the proof. The common conclusion for L = 1 is inconclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of equal cardinality (bijection criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sets A and B have the same cardinality, written |A| = |B|, if there exists a bijective function f : A → B. If no such bijection exists, then |A| ≠ |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition applies equally to finite and infinite sets; finding one bijection suffices to show equality. Bijections may be described by formulas, tables, or geometric constructions (examples given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion / method to show two sets have equal cardinality via bijection examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibit an explicit bijection f: A → B (e.g., f(n) = -n shows |{1,2,3,4}| = |{-1,-2,-3,-4}|; a table or formula describing each f(n) is acceptable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives multiple illustrative bijections (N ↔ Z via an explicit ordering, geometric bijection between (0,∞) and (0,1)). Use composition and inverses as needed; equality of cardinalities is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonal argument for non-surjectivity / uncountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any function f : N → R, construct a real number b whose nth decimal digit differs from the nth decimal digit of f(n); then b ≠ f(n) for every n, showing f is not surjective. Hence no surjection N → R exists and |N| ≠ |R|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constructive diagonalization is a general method to produce an element not in the image of an alleged surjection; used to prove the uncountability of R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of countable, countably infinite, and uncountable
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is countably infinite if |N| = |A| (there exists a bijection N → A). A set is countable if it is finite or countably infinite. A set is uncountable if it is infinite and there is no bijection N → A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, A is countably infinite iff its elements can be listed in an infinite sequence a1, a2, a3, .... Use this to prove sets like Q are countable by explicitly listing elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive listing method for Q (countability proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange rational numbers in a two-dimensional array (by numerator/denominator in reduced form) and traverse by a snake/path that hits every entry; this yields an explicit infinite list of Q, proving |Q| = |N|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove duplicates (non-reduced fractions) and follow a path that enumerates every reduced rational exactly once. This is a standard constructive technique to show countability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of countably infinite sets is countably infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are countably infinite, then A × B is countably infinite (Theorem 14.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: write A and B in lists and traverse the product grid along a diagonal/snake path (Figure 14.2) to enumerate A × B. Corollary: finite Cartesian products of countable sets are countable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of two countably infinite sets is countably infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are countably infinite, then A ∪ B is countably infinite (Theorem 14.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interleave elements (a1, b1, a2, b2, ...) and omit repeats. This gives a countable listing of the union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing cardinalities via injections/surjections (Definition 14.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: (1) |A| = |B| if there is a bijection A → B. (2) |A| < |B| means there is an injection A → B but no bijection A → B. (3) |A| ≤ |B| means there is an injection A → B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For finite sets this aligns with ordinary '<'. In general, establishing an injection or surjection is the primary tool for comparing infinite cardinalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's theorem on power sets (|A| < |P(A)|)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set A, |A| < |P(A)|. Equivalently, there is an injection f : A → P(A) (e.g., f(x) = {x}) but there is no surjection A → P(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the diagonal set B = {x ∈ A : x ∉ f(x)} to show no function f : A → P(A) can be surjective. This yields an infinite ascending chain of strictly larger cardinalities when iterated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite subset of a countably infinite set is countably infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is an infinite subset of a countably infinite set B, then A is countably infinite (Theorem 14.8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: list elements of B as b1, b2, ... and pick out those in A in order; the result is an infinite listing of A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncountable subset implies containing set uncountable
rubrics_metrics.description: If U ⊂ A and U is uncountable, then A is uncountable (Theorem 14.9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrapositive/contradiction: if A were countable then every subset would be at most countable, contradicting U uncountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor-Bernstein-Schroeder theorem (injection-both-ways criterion for equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exist injections f : A → B and g : B → A (i.e., |A| ≤ |B| and |B| ≤ |A|), then |A| = |B|; equivalently there exists a bijection h : A → B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem reduces proving equal cardinality to finding injections in both directions. The textbook presents an explicit construction (partition A into a set G and its complement W based on iterates of g∘f, then define h(x)=f(x) on G and h(x)=g^{-1}(x) on W) and proves injectivity & surjectivity of h.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive method (proof) for Cantor-Bernstein bijection
rubrics_metrics.description: Given injections f:A→B and g:B→A, define G = ⋃_{k≥0} (g∘f)^k(A − g(B)) and W = A\,G. Then define h(x)=f(x) if x∈G and h(x)=g^{-1}(x) if x∈W; this h is a bijection A→B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives the partitioning idea, checks well-definedness (elements of W lie in g(B) so g^{-1} defined), and verifies injectivity and surjectivity by cases. This is the standard constructive proof.
